claim: James Marshall found gold at Sutter's sawmill, Coloma, on January 24, 1848, on Nisenan and foothill Miwok land.
source_title: California State Parks, Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park brochure

claim: About 300,000 people came to California from 1848 to about 1855; almost 100,000 non-Natives by end of 1849.
source_title: Smithsonian NMAH, Many Voices: Gold Rush; PBS American Experience

claim: Most miners earned little: census-based study finds outcomes 'generally small or even zero for miners but... positive and large for nonminers'; average daily earnings fell from about $20 (1848) to about $6 (1852-53).
source_title: Clay and Jones, 'Migrating to Riches?', Journal of Economic History (2008)

claim: Real wages in California rose sharply 1848-1852, then declined.
source_title: Margo, 'Wages in California During the Gold Rush', NBER Historical Working Paper 101 (1997)

claim: 1849 prices: eggs and slices of bread about $1 each; boots costing $3-15 in the East sold for $30-40.
source_title: Smithsonian Magazine; PBS Food, 'Food of the California Gold Rush'

claim: Sam Brannan's store sold up to $5,000 in goods per day to miners; he was known as the richest man in California in the 1850s-60s.
source_title: PBS American Experience, 'Samuel Brannan'

claim: Levi Strauss went to San Francisco in 1853 to sell dry goods; the riveted jeans patent was granted May 20, 1873.
source_title: Levi Strauss & Co., 'The Story of Levi Strauss'

claim: 1850: $20/month on non-citizen miners (signed April 13, 1850; repealed March 14, 1851), mainly hit Latin American and French miners. 1852: $3/month, aimed at Chinese miners; raised to $4/month March 30, 1853.
source_title: PBS American Experience, 'Chinese Immigrants and the Gold Rush'; SCU Digital Exhibits

claim: About 4,000 mostly Mexican and Peruvian miners protested the 1850 tax at Sonora on May 19, 1850.
source_title: CUNY American Social History Project, 'Latin American and French Miners Protest the Foreign Miner's Tax'

claim: U.S. naturalization was limited to 'any Alien being a free white person', so Chinese immigrants could not become citizens.
source_title: Immigration History (UT Austin), Nationality Act of 1790

claim: 2,716 Chinese arrived in 1851 and 20,026 in 1852, following crop failures in southern China.
source_title: PBS American Experience, 'Chinese Immigrants and the Gold Rush'

claim: Hong Kong to San Francisco generally took ten to twelve weeks by sail (fast clippers 40-50 days); most migrants paid their own way or borrowed; the credit-ticket system existed but its extent is debated.
source_title: Mae Ngai, History News Network

claim: Sam Yup (1851) and Sze Yup (late 1851) district associations; Sze Yup met newcomers at the docks and provided housing, jobs and mining outfits; later the Six Companies (CCBA, formal 1882). Debt-tracking role not verified online.
source_title: PBS American Experience; NPS, 'The Chinese Six Companies'

claim: Governor John Bigler's special message on the 'Chinese Question', April 23, 1852, attacked 'Coolies' and called for heavy taxes.
source_title: Mae Ngai, History News Network

claim: Norman Asing's open letter in the Daily Alta California (early May 1852; May 5 per most scholars, May 15 per PBS): 'The declaration of your independence, and all the acts of your government, your people, and your history are all against you.'
source_title: PBS, Becoming American: The Chinese Experience

claim: People v. Hall, 4 Cal. 399 (1854): Chief Justice Murray held Chinese witnesses could not testify against white persons; George W. Hall's conviction for murdering Ling Sing was reversed.
source_title: CourtListener, People v. Hall; Immigration History

claim: Ling Sing, a Chinese miner in Nevada County, was killed in 1853; Chinese witnesses testified at Hall's trial.
source_title: SFSU Asian American/Pacific Islander biography project, Ling Sing

claim: The race-based testimony ban was dropped when California adopted its 1872 Penal Code.
source_title: Wikipedia summary of People v. Hall (secondary)

claim: Land Act of March 3, 1851: the Board of Land Commissioners heard 813 cases (1851-1856) and confirmed 604; with appeals, cases took an average of 17 years.
source_title: Online Archive of California, Bancroft Library finding aid, Documents Pertaining to the Adjudication of Private Land Claims

claim: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo lost most of his land to squatters and expensive legal proceedings.
source_title: University of Oklahoma Press, Recuerdos (Beebe and Senkewicz, trans.)

claim: Vallejo, Recuerdos (1875, Spanish, public domain): '¿a qué bien quejarnos? el mal está hecho y ya no tiene remedio.' Transcription not checked against the manuscript.
source_title: Peralta Hacienda Historical Park audio scripts

claim: California's Native population fell from perhaps 150,000 (1846/1848) to about 30,000 (1870/1873).
source_title: UCLA American Indian Studies Center, An American Genocide (Madley, Yale 2016); NMAI NK360

claim: Vigilantes, militiamen and soldiers killed between 9,492 and 16,094 California Indians (1846-1873); 370 massacres; 3,000-4,000 children forcibly transferred 1850-1868.
source_title: USC Center for Advanced Genocide Research, Madley lecture summary

claim: Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, April 22, 1850: allowed indenture of Indian children and adults, auction of 'vagrant' Indians; not fully repealed until 1937.
source_title: Johnston-Dodds, Early California Laws and Policies Related to California Indians, California State Library (2002)

claim: Governor Burnett, January 7, 1851: 'That a war of extermination will continue to be waged between the races, until the Indian race becomes extinct, must be expected.'
source_title: Johnston-Dodds (2002), citing Journals of the Senate and Assembly of the State of California, 1852, p. 15

claim: State militia expeditions against Indians cost $843,573.48 (1850-52); total claims $1,293,179.20 (1851-59); for 1854-59 expeditions the U.S. paid $229,987.67 of $449,605.74 claimed (Act of March 2, 1861). Congress reimbursed about $900,000 for early expeditions in 1854 (exact figure unconfirmed).
source_title: Johnston-Dodds (2002), Tables 1-2, from State Comptroller records, California State Archives

claim: Madley: state funding bills totaled about $1.5 million; Congress voted to reimburse about $900,000.
source_title: Anchorage Daily News, 2016 interview with Benjamin Madley

claim: Bloody Island, Clear Lake, May 15, 1850: U.S. soldiers killed Pomo people, mostly women, children and elders; estimates range about 60 to 200+.
source_title: California Office of Historic Preservation, Landmark No. 427

claim: Governor Newsom apologized to California Native Americans on June 18, 2019 (Executive Order N-15-19) and created a Truth and Healing Council.
source_title: Office of the Governor of California

claim: Dame Shirley, Indian Bar, April 10, 1852: 'Gold-mining is nature's great lottery scheme... It is a mere matter of chance.'
source_title: The Shirley Letters, Project Gutenberg #23280

claim: Dame Shirley, Indian Bar, May 1, 1852, on Rich Bar barring foreign miners: 'It seems to me that the above law is selfish, cruel, and narrow-minded in the extreme.'
source_title: The Shirley Letters, Project Gutenberg #23280

claim: Sarah Royce's A Frontier Lady was first published in 1932 (Yale); public-domain status not confirmed, so do not quote it in the game.
source_title: Library catalog record (NYPL)

claim: California became the 31st state on September 9, 1850, as part of the Compromise of 1850; its 1849 constitution banned slavery.
source_title: U.S. Senate, States in the Senate: California

claim: Gameloft's 2021 Oregon Trail hired Indigenous historians (Huettl, Phillips, Bauer) and added Native playable characters, removed stereotyped braids, bows and music.
source_title: NPR via KPBS, May 12, 2021

claim: Mission US 'A Cheyenne Odyssey' was developed with the Northern Cheyenne at Chief Dull Knife College, who consulted on content, script, design and casting.
source_title: Mission US, Process and Development

claim: EDC studies found Mission US knowledge gains (e.g., 15% pre/post gain vs under 1% control, 2016); no outcome study specific to A Cheyenne Odyssey found.
source_title: Mission US, Research and Outcomes

claim: 'Flight to Freedom' drew backlash in 2015 and October 2017 (Phoenix Elementary blocked it); no 2019 event found.
source_title: KJZZ (Phoenix public radio), October 2017

claim: Simulations of oppression 'trivialize the experience of the victims' and can put students 'in the position of defending and/or identifying with the oppressors'.
source_title: ADL, 'Why Simulation Activities Should Not Be Used'

claim: Learning for Justice warns simulations send the message 'Now you know what it feels like to be...'.
source_title: Learning for Justice, 'Classroom Simulations: Proceed With Caution' (2008)

claim: On Native history simulations and reenactments: 'These do tangible harm and naturalize the context as normal.' (Meredith McCoy, Carleton College)
source_title: K-12 Dive, October 2024

claim: NMAI NK360: 'There is no single American Indian culture or language'; teach Native nations as present-day.
source_title: Smithsonian Magazine, Sept 18, 2019

claim: NMAI inquiry lesson for grades 8-12 asks whether American actions against California Native Americans during the gold rush meet the UN definition of genocide.
source_title: NMAI Native Knowledge 360

claim: Children sharing one screen were more engaged with multiple input devices; one input device lets one child dominate.
source_title: Stewart, Bederson and Druin, Single Display Groupware (University of Maryland HCIL)
